steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an HCI paper on how data analysts understand and verify analyses produced by LLM-based AI assistants. It should motivate the problem, point out the gap in prior work, describe our design probe and user study, summarize findings and implications, and list contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Data analysis is hard; computation as a barrier
- LLM-based analysis assistants and the natural-language paradigm
- Challenge: AI errors, need for users to verify outputs
- Gap: prior HCI work on understanding LLM outputs ignores data analysis
- This work: HCXAI perspective, design probe, qualitative study
- Findings and implications
- Contributions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Data analysis is hard because practitioners need to combine their domain knowledge with computational expertise in order to get to reliable conclusions. For practitioners the computational challenges can be a barrier that keeps them from exploring alternative and valid analysis decisions, and so from doing robust analyses.

LLMs have improved a lot on programming tasks, both general ones, data science ones, and visualization ones. This suggests LLM-based analysis assistants as a promising solution, which lets data analysts execute and automate their analyses. Assistants like OpenAI’s Code Interpreter are now widely deployed, so there is a new paradigm emerging in how analysts do analyses. Analysts don't formulate the exact transformations and operations in the analysis anymore, instead they specify their analysis question as a natural language intent (Fig. 1 right). Then the AI assistant does the analysis task, it writes code to understand the data, makes the data transformations that are needed, and interprets the results. Many analysis tasks are time-consuming, even for analysts who know programming well, so natural language interactions can be more efficient, especially when the intent can be abstracted. Also, this natural language communication can make AI analysis tools more usable, so that they are accessible even to analysts who are not expert programmers.

But there is still a big challenge. AI-based assistants are powerful, but they can misinterpret what the user intends (see Fig. 1) or make outputs that seem correct but are erroneous. Misinterpretation is inherent in how flexible natural language communication is, so errors from existing AI-based assistants will probably persist no matter what the underlying LLM is. Conclusions from data analyses also often inform high-impact decisions in science, business, and government, so it is important that users of AI-based analysis assistants critically reflect on what the assistant outputs. In this new paradigm the focus of analysts shifts from writing and validating their own analyses to understanding and evaluating the analyses that AI assistants generate. This can be hard, since existing AI assistants don't have verification support and even experts can be susceptible to automation bias and overreliance.

- Gap
  - HCI work on understanding LLM outputs incl. AI code assistants; only programmers, not data analysis
  - analysis = iterative sensemaking of data; mental model of data + AI's procedure
  - Code Interpreter shows NL, Python code, comments, execution outputs; unclear how helpful
- This work
  - HCXAI perspective; study verification workflows, backgrounds, opportunities
  - prototype interface (Sec. 4), qualitative study with 22 professional analysts (Sec. 5), Table 1 datasets
  - queries by data scientists, presented as prompts written by an intern
- Findings: procedure-oriented -> data-oriented once issues noticed (Table 4); artifacts support each other (Fig. 5)
- Implications for analysts (Sec. 7.1) and designers (Sec. 7.2)
- Contributions (1) findings, (2) implications

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Data analysis is hard because practitioners need to combine their domain knowledge with computational expertise in order to get to reliable conclusions. For practitioners the computational challenges can be a barrier that keeps them from exploring alternative and valid analysis decisions, and so from doing robust analyses.

LLMs have improved a lot on programming tasks, both general ones, data science ones, and visualization ones. This suggests LLM-based analysis assistants as a promising solution, which lets data analysts execute and automate their analyses. Assistants like OpenAI’s Code Interpreter are now widely deployed, so there is a new paradigm emerging in how analysts do analyses. Analysts don't formulate the exact transformations and operations in the analysis anymore, instead they specify their analysis question as a natural language intent (Fig. 1 right). Then the AI assistant does the analysis task, it writes code to understand the data, makes the data transformations that are needed, and interprets the results. Many analysis tasks are time-consuming, even for analysts who know programming well, so natural language interactions can be more efficient, especially when the intent can be abstracted. Also, this natural language communication can make AI analysis tools more usable, so that they are accessible even to analysts who are not expert programmers.

But there is still a big challenge. AI-based assistants are powerful, but they can misinterpret what the user intends (see Fig. 1) or make outputs that seem correct but are erroneous. Misinterpretation is inherent in how flexible natural language communication is, so errors from existing AI-based assistants will probably persist no matter what the underlying LLM is. Conclusions from data analyses also often inform high-impact decisions in science, business, and government, so it is important that users of AI-based analysis assistants critically reflect on what the assistant outputs. In this new paradigm the focus of analysts shifts from writing and validating their own analyses to understanding and evaluating the analyses that AI assistants generate. This can be hard, since existing AI assistants don't have verification support and even experts can be susceptible to automation bias and overreliance.

In the HCI community, recent work looked at ways to give the user a better understanding of LLM-generated outputs, including the outputs of AI-based code assistants. But these studies only focus on programmers and not on data analysis specifically, so they miss a big portion of data analysts. Data analysis involves iteratively making sense of the underlying data, so analysts have to juggle their mental model of the data on top of their understanding of what the AI did. There is limited insight into how analysts with different programming skills and computational reasoning abilities go about this. Current code assistants like Open AI’s Code Interpreter show these steps in natural language, Python code, code comments, and code execution outputs. It is not clear how helpful these interface affordances are and how analysts use the different sources of information to check if AI-generated analyses are correct.

In this work we build on the perspective of recent work in Human-Centered Explainable AI (HCXAI), which is that users’ needs to understand AI-generated outputs depend on their backgrounds and their social and organizational contexts. We focus on data analysts and how they understand AI-assisted analyses. We study the verification workflows of analysts, how different backgrounds may influence their approaches, and opportunities to improve this experience. We want to guide the design of AI assistants that empower analysts to critically reflect on outputs generated by AI.

We developed a prototype interface to explore the behaviors of analysts and to get feedback on design opportunities (Sec. 4). It includes the AI’s code, code comments, and natural language explanation, and also additional interactive data tables and summary visualizations. This design accommodated a broad range of artifacts analysts might use during verification, so we could observe workflows that emerge naturally. Analysts could access intermediary data tables where they can filter, search, and sort for values to explore the data and verify the AI-generated output. We used our tool as a probe and conducted a qualitative study with 22 professional analysts (Sec. 5). We asked participants to verify AI-generated analyses that involved sequences of data transformations and covered a range of real-world datasets (Table 1). The analyses were generated in response to high-level analysis queries written by data scientists, and these were presented to participants as prompts written by an intern.

We found that analysts often started verifying with procedure-oriented behaviors (answering “what did the AI do?”) and then shifted to data-oriented behaviors (answering “does the [resulting] data make sense?”) once they noticed issues in the AI-generated output (Table 4). Analysts used procedure-oriented behaviors to get a high-level understanding of the analysis steps and to confirm low-level details in the data operations. Analysts used data-oriented behaviors to make sense of the data. Data artifacts (i.e., the data tables and summary visualizations) were often vital as secondary support in procedure-oriented behaviors, and it was the same the other way around for procedure artifacts (i.e., the natural language explanation and code/code comments) (Fig. 5).

Based on these findings (Sec. 6) we make recommendations for end-user analysts who interact with AI-based analysis assistants (Sec. 7.1). We also discuss implications for system designers (Sec. 7.2). These center around connecting data-oriented and procedure-oriented artifacts fluidly, communicating data operations and the AI’s assumptions about the data, and incorporating AI guidance into the verification workflows.

The contributions of this paper are:

- (1) Findings from a user study with our design probe that uncover common behavioral patterns in verifying AI-generated analyses,

- (2) A set of implications for end-user analysts interested in AI-assisted data analysis, together with design implications for tool builders to improve verification workflows.

steps.text:
Data analysis is challenging because practitioners must synthesize domain knowledge with computational expertise to draw reliable conclusions. For practitioners, computational challenges may act as a barrier to exploring alternative and valid analysis decisions, and therefore to conducting robust analyses [1,2].

Improved capabilities of large language models (LLMs) for general [3,4,5], data science [6,7,8], and visualization [9] programming tasks suggest LLM-based analysis assistants as a promising solution, letting data analysts execute and automate their analyses. Given the widespread deployment of assistants such as OpenAI’s Code Interpreter [10], an emerging paradigm is changing how analysts perform analyses. Rather than formulate the exact transformations and operations in an analysis, analysts specify their analysis question through a natural language intent (Fig. 1 right) [11]. The AI assistant then performs the analysis task: it writes code to understand the data, makes the necessary data transformations, and interprets the results. Since many analysis tasks are time-consuming [12,13,14,1], even for analysts well-versed in programming, natural language interactions can be more efficient, especially when the intent can be abstracted. Furthermore, natural language communication can broaden the usability of AI analysis tools, making them accessible even to analysts who are non-expert programmers [15].

Yet a significant challenge remains. AI-based assistants, while powerful, can misinterpret user intentions (see Fig. 1) [16,17,18] or produce seemingly correct but erroneous outputs [19,20]. Since misinterpretation is inherent in the flexibility of natural language communication [11,15,21], errors from existing AI-based assistants are likely to persist regardless of the underlying LLM. Moreover, because conclusions from data analyses often inform high-impact decisions in science [22,23], business [14,24,25], and government [26,27], it is important for users of AI-based analysis assistants to critically reflect on the assistant’s outputs [15]. In this new paradigm, analysts’ focus shifts from writing and validating their own analyses to understanding and evaluating the analyses generated by AI assistants [16]. This can be challenging, as existing AI assistants lack verification support [15,28] and even experts can be susceptible to automation bias and overreliance [29,30].

Recent work in the HCI community has explored ways to give users a better understanding of LLM-generated outputs, including those from AI-based code assistants [31,32]. However, these studies focus only on programmers and not on the specific domain of data analysis, missing a significant portion of data analysts [33,1]. Since data analysis involves iteratively making sense of the underlying data [34,35,36], analysts must juggle their mental model of the data in addition to their understanding of the AI’s procedure. There is limited insight into how analysts with different programming skills and computational reasoning abilities go about this process. Current code assistants such as Open AI’s Code Interpreter [10] present these steps in natural language, Python code, code comments, and code execution outputs. It is unclear to what extent these interface affordances help and how analysts use these different sources of information to assess the correctness of AI-generated analyses.

In this work, we build on the perspective of recent work in Human-Centered Explainable AI (HCXAI) [37,38,39,40] that users’ needs to understand AI-generated outputs depend on their backgrounds and their social and organizational contexts; we focus on data analysts as they understand AI-assisted analyses. We study analysts’ verification workflows, how different backgrounds may influence their approaches, and opportunities to improve this experience. We aim to guide the design of AI assistants that empower analysts to critically reflect on AI-generated outputs.

To explore analysts’ behaviors and elicit feedback on design opportunities, we developed a prototype interface that includes not only the AI’s code, code comments, and natural language explanation but also additional interactive data tables and summary visualizations (Sec. 4). This design accommodated a broad spectrum of artifacts that analysts may employ during verification, which let us observe naturally emerging workflows. Analysts could access intermediary data tables to filter, search, and sort for values to explore the data and verify the AI-generated output. Using our tool as a probe, we conducted a qualitative study with 22 professional analysts (Sec. 5). We asked participants to verify AI-generated analyses involving sequences of data transformations over a range of real-world datasets (Table 1). These analyses were generated in response to high-level analysis queries written by data scientists [7], which were presented to participants as prompts written by an intern.

We find that analysts often started their verification workflows with procedure-oriented behaviors (answering “what did the AI do?”) and shifted to data-oriented behaviors (answering “does the [resulting] data make sense?”) once they noticed issues in the AI-generated output (Table 4). Analysts adopted procedure-oriented behaviors to get a high-level understanding of the analysis steps and to confirm low-level details in the data operations, while they adopted data-oriented behaviors to make sense of the data. Notably, data artifacts (i.e., the data tables and summary visualizations) were often vital as secondary support in procedure-oriented behaviors, and vice versa for procedure artifacts (i.e., the natural language explanation and code/code comments) (Fig. 5).

Based on these findings (Sec. 6), we make recommendations to end-user analysts interacting with AI-based analysis assistants (Sec. 7.1), and we discuss implications for system designers (Sec. 7.2). These center around fluidly connecting data-oriented and procedure-oriented artifacts, communicating data operations and the AI’s assumptions about the data, and incorporating AI guidance into verification workflows.

This paper contributes the following:

- (1) Findings from a user study using our design probe that uncover common behavioral patterns in verifying AI-generated analyses,

- (2) A set of implications for end-user analysts interested in AI-assisted data analysis, paired with design implications for tool builders to improve verification workflows.
